entities.description: Historic Black newspaper founded in 1905 by Robert Sengstacke Abbott in Chicago; weekly 1905–1956, daily 1956–c.2008, weekly c.2008–2019, digital-only from July 2019. Owned by Sengstacke Enterprises Inc. (1940–2003) and Real Times Inc./Real Times Media (2003–present).

key_dates.start_note: Disputed day: BlackPast gives May 6; corpus position 'May 5, 1905 (BlackPast gives May 6)', dispute footnoted everywhere

entities.description: Founder, publisher, and editor of the Chicago Defender (1905–1940). One of the first African-American millionaires; creator of the Bud Billiken Club (1923).

entities.address: 3435 S. Indiana Ave., Chicago, IL 60616 (Douglas community area / Bronzeville)
entities.canonical_name: Chicago Defender Building (3435 S Indiana Ave)
entities.description: Defender headquarters 1920–1956 (building retained to 1960). Built 1899, designed by Henry L. Newhouse; originally Anshe Dorom synagogue. Designated a Chicago Landmark September 9, 1998 (Black Metropolis–Bronzeville District). DISTINCT FROM the newspaper organization.

key_dates.tenure_note: Harmonized composite: housed the paper 1920–1956 (building retained to 1960)

entities.description: Nephew of Robert S. Abbott; publisher of the Chicago Defender 1940–1997. Took the paper daily in 1956; built a four-paper chain; founded the National Negro Publishers Association (NNPA); served on Truman's 1948 armed-forces integration commission.

John H. Sengstacke's holding company for the Defender and its sister papers (Chicago Defender, Michigan Chronicle, Tri-State Defender, New Pittsburgh Courier). Placed in trust in 1975 with instructions to sell upon Sengstacke's death; sold 2002–2003.

entities.canonical_name: Real Times Inc. / Real Times Media
entities.description: Group led by Thom Picou (former Defender editor, Sengstacke's nephew) with Bobby Sengstacke and Detroit/Chicago investors; acquired Sengstacke Enterprises in a ~$10.9M probate-court-approved sale (approved Nov 4, 2002; control transferred January 2003). Owns the Defender today; Hiram E. Jackson was CEO at the 2019 digital transition.

entities.address: 2400/2410 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago, IL 60616 (Motor Row)
entities.description: Defender headquarters and printing plant ~1956–2003 (move completed by 1960; press operations ended ~2005). Former Illinois Automobile Club HQ, built 1936, designed by Prairie School architect Philip Maher; Olympic-size pool filled in to house printing presses. DISTINCT FROM the newspaper organization and from the 3435 S. Indiana building.

entities.address: 4445 S. Martin Luther King Jr. Dr., Chicago, IL 60653
entities.canonical_name: 4445 S. Martin Luther King Jr. Dr.
entities.description: Former Metropolitan Funeral Home in Bronzeville; Defender offices from May 2009 ('going back where we belong', president Michael House).

Informal distribution infrastructure by which Pullman porters carried Defender bundles on Southern rail routes and dropped them at barbershops and churches, circumventing local bans and newsstand exclusion. Corroborated core (Congressional Record); operational details (payment, routes, quantities, named agents) unresolved.

Movement of millions of Black Southerners to Northern and Midwestern cities, c.1915–1970. The Defender's Great Northern Drive (May 15, 1917) and sustained migration advocacy make the paper a documented catalyst; it did not single-handedly cause the migration.
Youth club founded 1923 by Abbott and managing editor Lucius Harper through the Defender's 'Defender Junior' children's page; encourages proper development and reading the Defender.
Nonprofit arm of the Defender; sponsors the Bud Billiken Day Parade and Picnic (since the 1940s) and youth/scholarship programs.

entities.canonical_name: Bud Billiken Day Parade and Picnic
entities.description: Annual South Side parade (first August 11, 1929) sponsored by Chicago Defender Charities; billed as the largest African-American parade in the U.S. (~1M attendees; 25M+ TV viewers reported; editions through at least 2025–2026).

key_dates.recurrence: annual, second Saturday of August; King Drive route, Washington Park festival

entities.description: Trade association of Black publishers, founded by John H. Sengstacke in Chicago in February 1940; later renamed the National Newspaper Publishers Association (still extant).
Detroit weekly established 1936 by John H. Sengstacke (first editor Louis E. Martin sent June 6, 1936; first-issue circulation 5,000); Sengstacke Enterprises sister paper.
Memphis weekly; grew out of the Defender's Memphis bureau in 1951; Sengstacke Enterprises sister paper.

Pittsburgh weekly relaunched 1967 after Sengstacke purchased the defunct Pittsburgh Courier's assets in 1965; Sengstacke Enterprises sister paper. Note: the Pittsburgh Courier itself is distinct from its successor.
Former Defender editor; John H. Sengstacke's nephew; organized and led the Real Times Inc. buyout of Sengstacke Enterprises (2002–2003); Real Times chairman/CEO.
John H. Sengstacke's surviving child; participant in the Real Times Inc. buyout.
CEO of Real Times Media (c.2019); announced the end of print and the digital-only move (July 2019).
Defender managing editor (1920s); co-created the Bud Billiken Club with Abbott (1923).
Defender reporter/associate editor 1951–1978; took over the one-person Washington, D.C. bureau in 1953 (correspondent to 1973); 'First Lady of the Black Press.'
Defender editor during WWII; the paper's first white (Jewish) editor; assembled the 'Victory Through Unity' edition.
Poet; early work published in the Defender in the 1930s; later the first African American to win a Pulitzer Prize in any category.
Founder of the Associated Negro Press (1919); previously a Chicago postal clerk and traveling ad salesman for the Chicago Defender.
Rival Black newspaper founded by Anthony Overton (Chicago). Documented as competitor context for the Defender; publication vs. its building (canon-chicago-bee-building) kept separate.

Family and business papers of the Defender's founding families: 83 boxes, ~4,000 photographs, ~100 home movies. Held at the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection, Chicago Public Library (Woodson Regional Library). Priority target for unresolved questions (agent contracts, porter mechanics).
